If you mean extracting chats that a user already had with ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, etc., then the approach depends on whether you're building your own application or trying to access the providers' consumer apps.

There are three main scenarios:

1. Your application uses the LLM APIs (Best way) ✅

If you're calling the APIs yourself, don't extract anything afterward.

Instead, store the conversation yourself before sending it to the model.

Example schema:

JSON
{
  "session_id": "chat_987654",
  "llm": {
    "provider": "openai",
    "model": "gpt-5.5"
  },
  "created_at": "2026-07-08T10:25:31Z",
  "messages": [
    {
      "id": "1",
      "role": "system",
      "text": "You are a helpful assistant.",
      "timestamp": "2026-07-08T10:25:31Z"
    },
    {
      "id": "2",
      "role": "user",
      "text": "Hello",
      "timestamp": "2026-07-08T10:25:40Z"
    },
    {
      "id": "3",
      "role": "assistant",
      "text": "Hi! How can I help?",
      "timestamp": "2026-07-08T10:25:41Z"
    }
  ]
}

Since you're generating every request yourself, you already know

session ID

provider

model

timestamps

token usage

latency

attachments

tool calls

No extraction is needed.

2. Extract chats from ChatGPT/Gemini/Claude web apps

This is much harder.

There is no official API that lets another application read a user's conversation history from these consumer chat apps.

Possible methods are:

A. Browser Extension ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

This is the cleanest method.

Your extension runs on

chatgpt.com
gemini.google.com
claude.ai

It can

read the DOM

intercept network requests

store conversations locally

export JSON

Example:

content.js

↓

DOM

↓

Extract messages

↓

Convert to JSON

↓

Save

This works for

ChatGPT

Claude

Gemini

Perplexity

Grok

if you write a parser for each.

B. Observe Network Requests ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

Most websites request conversation data as JSON.

Instead of scraping HTML, inspect the API calls.

For example,

Browser

↓

POST /backend-api/conversation

↓

JSON response

↓

Your extension intercepts it

The JSON usually already contains

conversation id

parent id

timestamps

author

content

metadata

This is much more reliable than scraping the rendered HTML.

C. DOM Parsing ⭐⭐⭐

If no suitable network response is available, parse the visible chat.

Example

<div data-message-author-role="user">

or

[data-message-author-role]

Read

role

text

timestamp

Build JSON.

3. Import exported chats

Most providers allow users to export their own data.

Example:

ChatGPT export

conversations.json

Claude export

json

Gemini export (via Google Takeout)

json/html

Your importer simply normalizes them.

Recommended Architecture
                 User
                   │
         ┌─────────┴──────────┐
         │                    │
   ChatGPT tab          Gemini tab
         │                    │
         └──── Browser Extension ────┐
                                     │
          Detect provider            │
          Read messages              │
          Session ID                 │
          Timestamp                  │
          Model                      │
                                     │
                         Normalize JSON
                                     │
                        Local Database
                                     │
                           Export JSON
Unified JSON Schema
JSON
{
  "provider": "openai",
  "llm_name": "gpt-5.5",
  "session_id": "abc123",
  "conversation_title": "Trip Planning",
  "created_at": "2026-07-08T09:00:00Z",
  "updated_at": "2026-07-08T09:20:00Z",
  "messages": [
    {
      "id": "m1",
      "role": "user",
      "text": "Hello",
      "timestamp": "2026-07-08T09:00:10Z"
    },
    {
      "id": "m2",
      "role": "assistant",
      "text": "Hi!",
      "timestamp": "2026-07-08T09:00:11Z"
    }
  ]
}

You can extend it with:

JSON
{
  "provider": "openai",
  "model": "gpt-5.5",
  "session_id": "...",
  "workspace": "...",
  "conversation_title": "...",
  "created_at": "...",
  "updated_at": "...",
  "message_count": 42,
  "messages": [
    {
      "id": "...",
      "parent_id": "...",
      "role": "user",
      "text": "...",
      "timestamp": "...",
      "attachments": [],
      "images": [],
      "files": [],
      "tool_calls": [],
      "citations": [],
      "tokens": {
        "prompt": 120,
        "completion": 300
      }
    }
  ]
}
If you need to support multiple providers

A modular parser design works well:

extractor/
│
├── base_parser.py
├── chatgpt_parser.py
├── gemini_parser.py
├── claude_parser.py
├── perplexity_parser.py
├── grok_parser.py
└── normalizer.py

Each provider parser implements methods like:

Python
Run
class BaseParser:
    def get_session_id(self): ...
    def get_model(self): ...
    def get_messages(self): ...
    def get_title(self): ...
    def get_metadata(self): ...

The normalizer converts provider-specific structures into your unified schema.

Efficiency tips

If you're building a browser extension, prefer this order:

Intercept the site's network responses (fastest and most complete when available).

Use any provider-exported JSON if the user imports their data.

Fall back to DOM parsing only when the needed data isn't available through network responses.

This approach minimizes parsing work, is generally more robust to UI changes, and preserves richer metadata (such as conversation IDs and model information) when the sites expose it to the browser. Keep in mind that these web apps can change their internal APIs and page structures at any time, so versioning your parsers and handling missing fields gracefully is important.
